name: The veil of Maya and ascetic salvation (Nirvana)
plain_explanation: Schopenhauer holds that the distinctness of one person from another is only an illusion ('the veil of Maya'); a good or wise person sees through this illusion via sympathy/love, recognizes that all suffering is ultimately one, and responds by turning away from willing altogether -- through complete chastity, voluntary poverty, fasting, and self-denial -- aiming at something like Buddhist Nirvana, which Schopenhauer interprets as extinction.
precise_definition: Schopenhauer's soteriology: since suffering results from the intensity of will, and the separateness of individuals is merely phenomenal (the 'veil of Maya'), the path to relief from suffering lies in the good man's loving, sympathetic insight into the unity of all things, which quiets and eventually denies his own will; practised fully (through asceticism, chastity, and self-torture), this leads toward a state Schopenhauer calls Nirvana, interpreted as the extinction of individual willing and, ultimately, of the phenomenal world itself as objectified will.
why_it_mattered: It is Schopenhauer's proposed 'way out' of cosmic suffering, explicitly modeled on Hindu and Buddhist doctrine rather than Christian doctrine, which he holds in generally low regard (though he still admires Christian mystics like Eckhart and the Christian doctrine of original sin).
historical_origin: The World as Will and Idea, Book IV; explicitly credited by Schopenhauer to Kant, Plato, and the Upanishads.
examples: Schopenhauer's ranking of Buddhism as 'the highest religion'
His hostility to what he calls the 'detestable doctrine of Islam'
The claim that after complete abolition of will, 'this our world... is nothing'
objections: Russell: it is 'not very consistent and not very sincere,' since the mystics Schopenhauer invokes sought positive union with God through contemplation, while Schopenhauer offers only a wholly negative goal (near-nonexistence), an interpretation Russell calls 'an insult to the mystics.'

Russell: so long as the sage exists at all, he still possesses will (which is evil), so he can only diminish, never eliminate, evil while alive -- making the doctrine's promised 'salvation' incoherent short of actual death, which Schopenhauer nonetheless says suicide cannot achieve.

Russell notes the doctrine is undercut by Schopenhauer's own life: he 'habitually dined well,' had many trivial love affairs, was quarrelsome and avaricious, and once threw an elderly seamstress downstairs, causing permanent injury and a court-ordered payment for the rest of her life.
competing_positions: Christian mysticism's positive goal of union with God, which Russell contrasts with Schopenhauer's purely negative 'nothingness'
influence_on_later_thinkers: Helped popularize Hindu and Buddhist ideas among European artistic and literary audiences.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Explicit and extensive engagement with Hindu, Buddhist, and Christian religious doctrine as rival paths to salvation.
